extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy / general educated readers interested in civilization and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic framework for judging a nation's degree of civilization by several 'powers' (conduct, knowledge, beauty, social life/manners) and by social conditions (equality, class structure, materialism). It compares France, England, Italy, Germany, and Scotland to illustrate how these elements interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of taste and aesthetic appreciation as a central element of a nation's humanization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italians are cited as preëminent in feeling the power of beauty; public judgment at shows (utterances like 'è brutto', 'è bello') often agrees with cultivated opinion. A strong public sense for beauty revives and sustains art and a 'serious and successful pursuit' of beauty. Lack of a sense for beauty limits civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of knowing things 'scientifically' and systematically — intellectual cultivation and respect for systematic knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germans exemplify this power; the criterion is not general culture but a strong commitment to knowing things by the right, regular process. A nation must value scientific, systematic knowledge for full humanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of social life and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of social intercourse and manners as a civilizing power that promotes equality and humane living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voltaire names the age of Louis XIV as bequeathing 'l'esprit de société' (the social spirit). France (and perhaps Athens) is praised for establishing a high ideal of social intercourse; humane manners make people feel like equals and spread agreeableness of life widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of conduct (moral conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral conduct — the habit and sense of right behaviour — regarded as the greatest element in humanization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asserts the power of conduct is the greatest of all powers; lacking it (as it argues France has) leaves a nation vulnerable to demoralization and intellectual stoppage. Conduct is distinct from social manners or philanthropy but essential for full civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance among the civilizing powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation's civilization depends on a balanced hold upon beauty, knowledge, social manners, and conduct rather than dominance of a single power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: France is given as an example: strong in social manners but weak in conduct, intellect, and beauty, producing both notable humanization in one line and serious dangers elsewhere. Reliance on one element alone (e.g., manners) is insufficient and can coincide with demoralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality as promoter of humanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Social equality fosters spread of social manners, refined perceptions, and a higher common standard of life across classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality in France helped diffuse refinement and agreeable life to many classes, and later produced political equality (the Revolution). The social spirit is 'a promoter of equality' and 'a community having humane manners is a community of equals.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-being should exceed mere material comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate ideal of well-being must be higher than simple material sufficiency; materialistic targets are an inadequate standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socialistic/communistic schemes fail when content with too low and material a standard of well-being; the 'instinct of perfection' resists a coarsened ideal. The essay cautions against accepting a purely material standard for civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public taste and informal aesthetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even illiterate or 'common' people can reliably judge beauty in public contexts — popular taste matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cardinal Antonelli's remark: Roman common people, though illiterate, judged beauty at public shows in agreement with cultivated opinion. This supports counting popular taste as part of a nation's aesthetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of material well-being affects civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: How widely material comfort is spread influences social refinement and the capacity for humane life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belgian economist M. de Laveleye notes France's widespread material wellbeing (soil division, increased wealth, controlled population) helps explain its social refinement among peasantry. Material prosperity distributed widely aids agreeable social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Puritanism/narrow religiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: A focus on conduct and narrow religious seriousness can produce a hideous, ennui-stricken culture lacking beauty, intellect, and social charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English Puritan temper exemplifies this: strong for conduct but deficient in beauty, knowledge, and manners. Historical examples (Parliament selling/burning art; Milton's contentious tone) show how such a temper impoverishes national culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of the aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy can fix standards of manners and cultivate refinement, but when 'materialized' it becomes a source of vulgarization and loses civilizing function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically aristocracies had positive social functions; in the modern world those functions are gone and large estates often foster mere luxury. A materialized aristocracy is out of touch with large spiritual movements and undermines the pursuit of beauty and higher aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of class imitation and visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Visible splendor of a higher class can demoralize or set unreachable standards for lower classes, producing vulgar admiration rather than genuine civilizing aspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spectacle of aristocratic wealth tempts middle and lower classes into materialistic ideals ('admiring and worshipping the splendid materiality'), thereby reinforcing vulgarity and brutality rather than elevating standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties and responsibilities of the middle class
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle class contains a serious portion that sustains conduct and a gay/rowdy portion; overall it needs a better ideal of life to become a true civilizing force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The serious middle class preserved conduct but was imprisoned by Puritanism for two hundred years, producing narrowness and 'immense ennui.' The essay argues the middle class must transform and adopt broader ideals (intellect, beauty, manners) to advance civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization observable in everyday pleasures and sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: Compatibility in everyday pleasures, recreations, eating and drinking indicates humane life across classes and is a sign of civilized society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French peasantry can converse and share pleasures with cultivated people, unlike many English lower or middle-class settings where such compatibility is lacking; this everyday sociability is evidence of a humane life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of materialism to intellectual openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Materialism narrows horizons, reduces openness and flexibility of mind, and limits the play of ideas necessary for civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'materialism which they see regnant' blocks mental horizon for classes (including the cultivated gentleman class contiguous to aristocracy). Materialized classes tend to lack faith, ardor, and effective civilizing influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a new ideal of life for social reorganization
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's present organization must yield once the middle class acquires a better (broader, less materialistic) ideal of life; only then can civilization progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The current social stage has been useful but is over; the middle class must be provided with a better ideal of life than at present, else society will 'flounder' and face standstill despite many good efforts.
